thread.title: What We Learned From Big Tech Earnings - Barron's

author: Jon Swartz
title: What We Learned From Big Tech Earnings - Barron's
text:
By Jon Swartz May 1, 2018 5:30 p.m. ET Illustration: Bloomberg News The View From Silicon Valley
What we learned from big tech earnings the past week, culminating in Apple's results today, for good and ill:
Amazon.com (AMZN) appears to be in the pole position to become the first public company to reach $1 trillion in market value .
Its astonishing first-quarter performance —it rang up $1.6 billion in profits off the growing strength of its Amazon Web Services division—could well put it on the path to reach $2,000 per share and attain 13 digits.
Two other factors, among many, are likely to accelerate revenue. Amazon jacked up the price of its Prime service to $119 from $99 a year for its more than 100 million subscribers, and it reported $2 billion in advertising under the category of "other." The latter development has prompted some analyst chatter that Amazon could soon challenge the digital advertising dominance of Alphabet’s (GOOGL) Google and Facebook (FB).
Ben Schachter , an analyst at investment bank Macquarie , predicted as much Friday. He raised Amazon’s 12-month price forecast to a new target of $2,100, which would take it to a record $1.02 trillion.
As the Seattle-based company rises, Apple (AAPL), currently the highest-valued company at $833 billion, is falling. Blame it on iPhone .
On Tuesday, it announced second-quarter results of $2.73 earnings per share on $61.1 billion in revenue, both were in line with analysts' estimates. The company raised its dividend 16% and announced a $100 billion stock buyback. Apple sold 52.2 million iPhones in the March quarter, up 3% from the same quarter a year ago but shy of analysts' estimates.
That's all well and good—until the focus switched to projected iPhone sales in June, which are very bad. Katy Hubert , managing director of research at Morgan Stanley , reduced her iPhone shipment estimates in the June quarter from 40.5 million to 34 million. (Apple sold 41 million iPhones in the year-ago June quarter.)
The news is particularly vexing in China , where Apple has lost up to half its market share the past few years, according to various market researcher reports. Apple's market share is down to about 18%, says Morgan Stanley .
Sales of iPhones tell the story. They peaked at 71 million in the Greater China region in 2015, but have declined in successive years to 59 million, 49 million, and a predicted 47 million in 2018. UBS estimates Apple's share of top-tier users in China has plummeted to 20% to 30% today from 40% to 50% in 2015.
Perhaps the proverbial silver lining is in AR/VR , if rumors of a mixed-reality headset from Apple in 2020 are true. The company could use a revenue-producing alternative in addition to the iPhone, which accounts for 60% of sales, and Services .
A key question for Apple remains, How long can it continue to grow if its increased revenue is directly tied to iPhone price hikes, such as the $1,000 iPhone X?
Alphabet continued its steady beat of easily beating analysts' estimates . First-quarter revenue jumped 26% to $27.76 billion, producing EPS of $9.93.
In addition to typically strong advertising revenue, it posted a 36% gain in sales for "other" (mobile devices, speakers) to $4.35 billion, and a 14% improvement in "other bets" (self-driving cars) to $150 million—underscoring revenue diversification beyond advertising. This is important, financial analysts stress, because Google and Facebook will inevitably face regulatory pressure that could eventually impact ad sales.
Facebook, meanwhile, saved face from its embarrassing imbroglio with political consultancy Cambridge Analytica to post dazzling results.
(Photo by Carl Court/Getty Images) Illustration: Getty Images The social-networking giant's ability to seemingly shrug off the scandal was illustrated in its first-quarter results . It reported better-than-expected earnings of $1.69 per share and a 49% jump in revenue, almost all of it advertising, to $11.97 billion.
Goldman Sachs analyst Heather Bellini expected "little or no impact" on advertising spending from the Cambridge Analytica privacy scandal. She was right: Facebook said ad sales soared 50% to $11.8 billion for Q1.
The proof is in the shares: After a taking a beating on Wall Street and Capitol Hill for weeks, Facebook's stock is nearly back to the price where it started in 2018.
Which brings us, finally, to Microsoft (MSFT). Its third-quarter numbers breezed past analyst estimates, but lack of growth in the server software business dinged its stock last Thursday.
The takeaway? In the race to reach $1 trillion, Amazon, for now, is in pole position for the short and long term. But don't count out Apple and Alphabet.
